problem: Traditional semantic maps rely on fixed symbolic vocabularies, and existing open-vocabulary exploration methods depend on 2D maps or expensive ray-casting over TSDF submaps to score candidate views, which does not scale on resource-constrained robots.
motivation: Robots need to search for arbitrary objects and abstract concepts given by natural language in partially unknown environments. Good observation poses depend on occlusion and semantic orientation, not on geometry alone, and no dataset of best view poses exists, so a cheap learned view scorer is needed.
key_idea: Augment a 3D scene graph with CLIP embeddings for open-set queries, and train a self-supervised View Quality Estimation network that scores candidate observation poses directly from the graph, without online ray-casting, to guide semantic frontier exploration.
insight: The authors report that good views are not a function of geometry alone: simple heuristics (viewing angle, distance to centroid) fail in cluttered scenes, and 2D maps are insufficient. Directly regressing poses via differentiable rendering fell into local minima that were geometrically valid but semantically meaningless, which motivated regressing quality scores for sampled candidates instead. These are qualitative observations from initial experiments; no ablations are reported.
method: Open-set 3DSSG: a hierarchical heterogeneous 3D scene graph (objects to rooms) extended with CLIP feature vectors per node; class-agnostic segmentation (SAM/FastSAM) of RGB-D frames, CLIP embedding of masks, and preference for views where the object is clearly visible.

Text querying: a query embedding is compared with node embeddings by cosine similarity and all matching objects are returned; higher-order concepts (e.g. kitchenette) are obtained by clustering low-level objects using the graph hierarchy.

View Quality Estimation (VQE): a neural network predicts a query-relative quality score for uniformly sampled candidate poses around a target, taking partially mapped objects and their context from the 3DSSG; this replaces ray-casting.

Self-supervised training: in Habitat with HM3D, semantic maps are built from GT trajectories; query-map pairs are sampled, top-k regions are retrieved, views are rendered from GT meshes, embedded by a frozen CLIP, and a cosine-loss variant against the query embedding is back-propagated.
Planned exploration: learned view proposals are prioritized to verify known or hypothesized targets, falling back to semantically weighted frontier exploration for unknown regions.

Demonstrator: a TIAGo robot with Ouster OS0 LiDAR and Femto Bolt RGB-D camera, localized against pre-recorded maps with MICP-L, which also allows filtering of panoptic classes like walls and ceilings.

setting.backbone: CLIP (frozen) + class-agnostic segmentation (SAM/FastSAM) + VQE network (trained, architecture unspecified)
setting.training_data: Self-supervised on maps and rendered views generated from HM3D scenes in Habitat; no scale reported
setting.observation: RGB-D frames with pose (GT trajectories in simulation; LiDAR localization on the real robot)
setting.action_space: Candidate observation poses in map coordinates plus frontier targets (planned)
setting.privileged: GT trajectories and semantic annotations for map building and GT meshes for rendering during training; pre-recorded high-resolution maps for localization on the real robot

numbers_note: Project report with no quantitative results; the full pipeline evaluation is stated as future work.
results: No quantitative results are reported. The paper presents the architecture, qualitative CLIP query examples on the VL map, and a localization demonstration on the TIAGo robot. Findings are qualitative design insights.
limitations: No quantitative evaluation or benchmark results; the full exploration pipeline is not yet tested, including on the real robot.
Keeping instance geometry consistent under sensor noise in a 3DSSG is harder than in unified TSDF/voxel maps, which are also more efficient for visibility checks.
The VQE architecture and training details are not specified, and the training signal depends on CLIP similarity of renderings, which may not reflect true view usefulness.
